q: In most of the musical instruments, the stretched strings act as a source of sound.
e: True. In most of the musical instruments, the stretched strings act as a source of sound. A string fixed at both ends has nodes at the ends. The fundamental wavelength is 2L.

q: When the stretched strings are plucked, progressive waves are produced.
e: False. A string fixed at both ends has nodes at the ends. The fundamental wavelength is 2L.

q: When the string is plucked, the stationary waves with nodes at the fixed ends are formed.
e: True. When the string is plucked, the stationary waves with nodes at the fixed ends are formed. Standing waves stay put with nodes and antinodes. Progressive waves travel and carry energy.

q: When the string is plucked, the stationary waves with antinodes at the fixed ends are formed.
e: False. The claim puts antinodes where nodes belongs. When the string is plucked, the stationary waves with nodes at the fixed ends are formed. Antinodes are the peaks of vibration, midway between nodes.

q: The waves that are formed on the string are called harmonics.
e: True. The waves that are formed on the string are called harmonics. Harmonics are integer multiples of the fundamental frequency.

q: For the $n^{th}$ harmonic, the wavelength is given by $\lambda_n = rac{2l}{n}$ where $n=1, 2, 3, ...$.
e: True. For the n^th harmonic, the wavelength is given by λ_n = rac{2l}{n} where n=1, 2, 3,. Keep the symbols and the sign in that relation.

q: For the $n^{th}$ harmonic, the wavelength is given by $\lambda_n = rac{l}{n}$ where $n=1, 2, 3, ...$.
e: False. The claim puts rac{l}{n} where rac{2l}{n} belongs. For the n^th harmonic, the wavelength is given by λ_n = rac{2l}{n} where n=1, 2, 3,.

q: The corresponding frequencies are calculated from $v = f_n \lambda_n$, where $v$ is the velocity of the wave in a string.
e: True. The corresponding frequencies are calculated from v = f_n λ_n, where v is the velocity of the wave in a string. Keep the symbols and the sign in that relation.

q: The frequencies of a vibrating string of length $l$ are given by $f_n = rac{nv}{2l}$ where $n=1, 2, 3, ...$.
e: True. The frequencies of a vibrating string of length l are given by f_n = rac{nv}{2l} where n=1, 2, 3,. Keep the symbols and the sign in that relation.

q: Vibration of a string in one single segment is called the fundamental or first harmonic.
e: True. Vibration of a string in one single segment is called the fundamental or first harmonic. The fundamental is the lowest standing-wave frequency. Higher ones are harmonics or overtones.

q: Vibration of a string in one single segment is called the first overtone.
e: False. The claim puts first where fundamental belongs. Vibration of a string in one single segment is called the fundamental or first harmonic. Harmonics are integer multiples of the fundamental frequency.

q: A musical tone which is part of the harmonic series above a fundamental note is called an overtone.
e: True. A musical tone which is part of the harmonic series above a fundamental note is called an overtone. The fundamental is the lowest standing-wave frequency. Higher ones are harmonics or overtones.

q: The velocity of a wave in a vibrating string depends on the tension of the string and mass per unit length of the string.
e: True. The velocity of a wave in a vibrating string depends on the tension of the string and mass per unit length of the string. velocity has to stay in that role in the sentence.

q: The velocity of a wave in a vibrating string is given by the formula $v = \sqrt{ rac{T}{\mu}}$.
e: True. The velocity of a wave in a vibrating string is given by the formula v = √( rac{T}{μ}). Keep the symbols and the sign in that relation.

q: The velocity of a wave in a vibrating string is given by the formula $v = \sqrt{ rac{\mu}{T}}$.
e: False. The claim puts rac{μ}{t} where rac{t}{μ} belongs. The velocity of a wave in a vibrating string is given by the formula v = √( rac{T}{μ}).

q: In the formula $v = \sqrt{ rac{T}{\mu}}$, $T$ represents the tension of the string.
e: True. In the formula v = √( rac{T}{μ}), T represents the tension of the string. Keep the symbols and the sign in that relation.

q: In the formula $v = \sqrt{ rac{T}{\mu}}$, $\mu$ represents the total mass of the string.
e: False. In the formula v = √( rac{T}{μ}), T represents the tension of the string.

q: The frequencies of the vibrating string can also be written in terms of $T$ and $\mu$ as $f_n = rac{n}{2l} \sqrt{ rac{T}{\mu}}$.
e: True. The frequencies of the vibrating string can also be written in terms of T and μ as f_n = rac{n}{2l} √( rac{T}{μ}). Keep the symbols and the sign in that relation.

q: For the second harmonic, $n=2$, the frequency is $f_2 = 2f_1$.
e: True. For the second harmonic, n=2, the frequency is f_2 = 2f_1. Frequency is the number of turns per second, the reciprocal of the period.

q: For the third harmonic, $n=3$, the frequency is $f_3 = 3f_1$.
e: True. For the third harmonic, n=3, the frequency is f_3 = 3f_1. Frequency is the number of turns per second, the reciprocal of the period.

q: Mass per unit length of the string is the ratio of mass to length of the string.
e: True. Mass per unit length of the string is the ratio of mass to length of the string. Mass has to stay in that role in the sentence.
